title: The N+1 Query Problem and Batching (DataLoader)
lesson:
The N+1 query problem happens when code fetches a list with one query and then issues one additional query per item to load related data. Rendering 100 orders and then fetching each order's customer separately costs 101 round trips. Each query may be fast on its own, but the per-query network latency, connection checkout, and parsing overhead add up linearly with list size, and the database sees a burst of tiny queries instead of one efficient one.

It is easy to introduce accidentally. ORMs with lazy loading hide the extra query behind an innocent attribute access, and GraphQL resolvers invite it because each field resolver runs independently per parent object. It is usually invisible in development with 5 rows and painful in production with 5,000. The reliable way to catch it is to count queries per request in tests or tracing, and alert when a request's query count grows with its result size.

There are two main fixes. Eager loading uses a JOIN or a second query with a WHERE id IN (...) clause to fetch all related rows at once, which is 2 queries instead of N+1. The JOIN form can multiply rows and transfer duplicated parent data when relationships are one-to-many, so the IN form is often preferred for those. The second fix, common in GraphQL, is request-scoped batching as implemented by DataLoader: resolvers call load(id), the loader collects all keys requested during the same tick of the event loop, issues a single batched query, and hands each caller its own result. It also caches per request so duplicate keys are fetched once.

Batching has limits. Very large IN lists can hit parameter limits or produce poor query plans, so batches are often capped and split. Batching also adds a small delay while keys are collected, and loaders must be created per request so one user's cached data is never served to another.

questions.prompt: A page loads 50 posts with one query, then runs one query per post to load its author. How many queries run?
questions.explanation: One query for the list plus one per item is N+1, here 1 + 50 = 51.

questions.prompt: N+1 problems are usually obvious in development because each extra query is slow.
questions.explanation: Each query is typically fast and dev datasets are tiny, so the problem only becomes visible as result sizes grow in production.

questions.prompt: DataLoader collects keys requested in the same event-loop tick and issues one ____ query for all of them.
questions.explanation: Batching turns many per-key lookups into a single query that serves all callers.

questions.prompt: Why should a DataLoader instance be created per request rather than shared globally?
options: To reduce memory for the event loop
To avoid serving one user's cached data to another and avoid stale cache across requests
Because batching only works with one key
questions.explanation: The loader's cache is only safe within a single request's scope, where authorization and freshness are consistent.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of how a DataLoader resolves per-item lookups, earliest first.
items: One batched query runs with all collected keys
Each result is returned to the resolver that asked for its key
Resolvers call load(id) for each parent item
Loader waits until the current event-loop tick ends
questions.explanation: Keys are gathered during the tick, fetched in one query, then fanned back out to individual callers.
